To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
stomatal conductance is sensitive to vapour pressure difference when gas exchange measurements are made in the absence of CO 2 or at low partial pressures of CO2.

stomatal responses to a change in VPD between leaf and air are present in the three species tested, Gossypium, Glycine, and Xanthium, at ambient CO 2 partial pressure (39-41 Pa) and at partial pressures of CO2 below the CO2 compensation point.

stomata respond to a change of vapour pressure difference (VPD) between leaf and air even at near-zero partial pressures of carbon dioxide (CO 2) when CO 2 compensation points are below the VPD of the air.
In summary, our research is concerned with
stomatal responses to changes vapour pressure difference (VPD) between leaf and air, and the effect of CO 2 concentration on stomatal sensitivity to VPD.
the effect of vapour pressure difference on stomatal aperture.

a better understanding of the mechanisms of stomatal responses to changes of vapour pressure differences between leaf and air, and how these responses may be modified by changes in ambient carbon dioxide partial pressures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

stomatal conductance to H 2 O is a function of both leaf to air vapour pressure difference and CO 2 concentration, but the relative contribution of each of these variables to the total stomatal response is a function of CO 2 concentration.
the stomatal response to a change in leaf-to-air vapour pressure difference is dependent upon the partial pressure of CO 2 in the gas phase.
the stomatal response to a change in VPD between leaf and air is not a function of the CO2 partial pressure of the gas phase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stomata respond to changes in vapoured water flux between leaf and air and that stomata are sensitive to changes in vapours of water and carbon dioxide.

stomatal responses to changes of vapour pressure difference are not eliminated at near-zero CO 2 partial pressures, but are modified in a manner that is consistent with the hypothesis that stomata are sensitive to a change in water potential of the leaf.

the stomatal response to changes in vapur pressure difference is independent of the ambient partial pressure of CO 2, but that the stomatal sensitivity to a change in vapor pressure difference is affected by the partial pressure of CO2 in the ambient air.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stomata are responsive to a change in the water vapour concentration gradient between leaf and air, regardless of the ambient partial pressure of CO 2.
stomatal responses to a change in leaf-to-air vapour pressure difference are not eliminated at near-zero carbon-dioxide partial pressures.

we should not be surprised if we observe stomatal responses to a change in leaf-air vapour pressure difference when we measure stomatal conductance of leaves at ambient CO 2 partial pressures (40 Pa) and below the CO2 compensation point.
